verdict.rationale: ROS 2 ships its own SROS2/DDS-Security layer that controls communications across the ROS graph. Security enclaves each hold a single protection policy and can be mapped to processes, users, or devices, which gives a graph-level way to govern who can participate. This is not an operator-facing roles-and-permissions system, and the evidence never shows per-robot command, configure, or view privileges assigned to human roles. Missing for 10: role definitions for human operators, documented separation of command vs. configure vs. view permissions per robot, any management UI or workflow, and independent or hands-on corroboration.

support.subject: As an ops lead, I can control with roles and permissions who is allowed to command, configure, or view each robot

citations.quote: A security enclave encapsulates a single policy for protecting ROS communications.
Security enclaves can be flexibly mapped to processes, users, or devices at deployment.
Built-in ROS 2 security features enable control over communications throughout the ROS graph.
The `sros2` package provides the tools and instructions to use ROS 2 on top of DDS-Security.
